title: Digital incentives are preferred by most people, but physical cash remains important for a smaller lower-income group
source_unit: Census Research Report Series nonprobability survey experiment asking preferences for $5 and $40 incentive payments
geography: United States; large nonprobability survey of adults

observations.period: 2026 survey of promised incentive preferences; paper published May 2026

denominator.unit: large nonprobability survey respondents; exact sample count not disclosed in the landing-page abstract

cash_preference.value: about 5% preferred physical cash for either the $5 or $40 incentive

digital_preference.value: most respondents preferred electronic bank transfers or digital gift cards

cash_subgroup.value: the small group preferring cash was mostly young, low-income, and without a college degree

incentive_options.value: vignettes compared cash, digital gift cards, physical gift cards, checks, and electronic bank transfers for $5 and $40

observations.method: A large nonprobability survey asked respondents which of five payment forms they would prefer for two incentive amounts; the study compares preference patterns across respondent subgroups.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census survey-methods working paper using a nonprobability survey. The landing-page abstract does not disclose the exact sample count, weighting, response process, actual payment behavior, device access, bank access, fees, or whether stated preferences predict completed receipt.
observations.subgroup: Respondents grouped by age, income, and educational attainment; the abstract identifies the cash-preferring subgroup as mostly young, low-income, and without a college degree.
observations.counterinterpretation: A preference for digital transfer or gift cards may reflect convenience, but could also reflect the specific options, amount, trust, fees, bank access, phone access, or inability to use cash in a particular setting. Stated preference is not successful receipt or household benefit.

related_sources.claim: The Census Household Panel text-contact study adds a separate digital-access and consent layer; it does not measure incentive-payment preference or receipt.

boundary: This record adds a stated-payment-preference and digital-access pathway. It does not establish actual payment receipt, affordability, bank or device access, privacy, incentive effectiveness, survey response, or household security.
